question: What is the main difference between pre-gestational diabetes and gestational diabetes?

options.A: Insulin is strictly forbidden for treating the condition
options.B: It only occurs during the final trimester of pregnancy
options.C: The mother does not require any dietary modifications
options.D: The condition is present before the pregnancy begins

explanation: Pre-gestational diabetes means the woman already had diabetes prior to conception, whereas gestational diabetes starts during the pregnancy. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why does pre-gestational diabetes carry high risks during early pregnancy?

options.A: Organ formation happens during the first weeks when blood sugar may be unmanaged
options.B: Fetal kidneys stop functioning before the twelfth week
options.C: The placenta produces too much insulin to counter the high glucose
options.D: Maternal weight drops suddenly during the first trimester

explanation: Major fetal organs form very early in pregnancy, so high blood glucose during this critical window can lead to birth defects. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h1)

question: What is the main cause of Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Temporary resistance of tissues to normal insulin
options.B: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.C: Severe dietary deficiency of essential minerals
options.D: Excessive hormone production by the placenta

explanation: Type 1 diabetes occurs when the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which treatment is essential for a pregnant woman with Type 1 diabetes?
explanation: Because the pancreas produces little to no insulin in Type 1 diabetes, external insulin is essential for survival and managing blood sugar. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h2)

question: How does high maternal blood sugar cause a baby to grow very large?

options.A: High blood sugar stops the fetus from burning any stored body fat
options.B: The placenta stores extra amniotic fluid that makes the baby gain water weight
options.C: Maternal red blood cells cross the placenta and increase the baby's muscle mass
options.D: Extra glucose causes the fetus to produce more insulin, which drives rapid growth

explanation: Excess glucose stimulates the fetal pancreas to pump out extra insulin, and insulin promotes fat storage and body growth in the baby. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct effect of high maternal blood glucose on the fetus?

options.C: High glucose levels in fetal blood

explanation: High maternal blood sugar actually causes an INCREASE in fetal insulin production, not a decrease. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why are birth defects more common in babies born to mothers with poorly controlled pre-gestational diabetes?

options.A: High glucose disrupts normal tissue formation during early embryonic development
options.B: Maternal blood pressure drops too low during the first trimester
options.C: The placenta blocks essential vitamins from reaching the growing embryo
options.D: The umbilical cord wraps around the baby's limbs early on

explanation: High blood sugar acts as a teratogen during the first few weeks when organs are forming, leading to structural birth defects. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h4)

question: A woman at 36 weeks with pre-gestational diabetes has an ultrasound showing a very large baby and high amniotic fluid. What condition should the midwife expect?
explanation: Excess fetal growth is macrosomia, and high amniotic fluid is polyhydramnios, both classic findings in poorly controlled diabetic pregnancies. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h4)

question: What does an HbA1c test measure in a woman with diabetes?

options.A: Total amount of daily insulin produced by the pancreas
options.B: Rate at which the kidneys filter waste products from blood
options.C: Current blood glucose level at the exact moment of the test
options.D: Average blood sugar levels over the past two to three months

explanation: HbA1c measures hemoglobin with attached glucose, giving a reliable picture of blood sugar control over the preceding 8 to 12 weeks. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why is pre-conception counseling especially important for women with pre-gestational diabetes?

options.A: It prevents the placenta from forming during the first trimester
options.B: It allows time to achieve good blood sugar control before organ formation begins
options.C: It guarantees the baby will be born exactly on the estimated due date
options.D: It is the only time oral diabetes medications can be safely prescribed

explanation: Good blood sugar control before pregnancy dramatically lowers the rate of major birth defects that occur during early embryonic development. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the main goal of blood glucose monitoring during pregnancy for diabetic women?

options.A: Maintaining near-normal blood sugar levels without causing severe hypoglycemia
options.B: Completely eliminating the need for any carbohydrate intake in diet
options.C: Predicting the exact birth weight of the baby down to the gram
options.D: Ensuring the mother's pancreas starts producing insulin again

explanation: The main aim is tight control to protect the fetus while keeping the mother safe from dangerously low blood sugar. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why are pregnant women with diabetes advised to eat small, frequent meals instead of three large ones?

options.A: It helps prevent large spikes and drops in blood glucose levels
options.B: Small meals ensure the baby absorbs all protein consumed
options.C: Frequent eating prevents excessive weight gain in the mother
options.D: Large meals stop the placenta from functioning properly

explanation: Spreading food intake throughout the day avoids sudden surges in blood sugar that are hard to manage with insulin. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h6)

question: Why is an intravenous insulin and glucose infusion often used during labor for a diabetic mother?

options.A: To speed up cervical dilation and shorten the first stage of labor
options.B: To stop the uterus from having strong contractions
options.C: To replace the fluids lost from severe morning sickness
options.D: To keep maternal blood sugar stable and prevent low blood sugar in the newborn

explanation: Managing maternal blood sugar tightly during labor prevents the baby from having high insulin levels that cause sudden drops in newborn blood sugar after birth. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h7)

question: When is delivery usually planned for a well-controlled pre-gestational diabetic pregnancy?

options.A: During the 32nd week to avoid any signs of macrosomia
options.B: Between 38 and 39 weeks to balance risks of stillbirth and prematurity
options.C: Strictly at 42 weeks to ensure the lungs are fully mature
options.D: Whenever the mother goes into spontaneous labor regardless of date

explanation: Continuing pregnancy past term carries higher risks of stillbirth in diabetic pregnancies, so delivery is usually planned around 38 to 39 weeks. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h7)

question: Why do insulin requirements drop dramatically right after the placenta is delivered?

options.A: Breastfeeding instantly cures both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes
options.B: The baby's pancreas starts supplying insulin to the mother
options.C: Placental hormones that cause insulin resistance are suddenly removed
options.D: The mother stops eating for several days following childbirth

explanation: The placenta produces hormones that resist insulin; once delivered, insulin sensitivity returns quickly, lowering the required dose. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h8)

question: What is a common metabolic problem to watch for in a newborn delivered by a mother with pre-gestational diabetes?

options.A: Chronic high blood pressure requiring medication
options.B: Permanent inability to digest breast milk proteins
options.C: Severe dehydration from lack of body fluids
options.D: Hypoglycemia due to ongoing high insulin production

explanation: The baby's high insulin levels continue for a short time after birth even though the supply of maternal glucose has stopped, causing low blood sugar. [learn more](BMP221_U4_T3#BMP221_U4_T3_h8)
